ask.title: Ask your agent
ask.lede: Every computer comes with its own agent. Tell it what to build, watch its progress, and answer its questions in the Agent panel.
ask.keyNote: {{keys}} opens or closes the Agent panel from any page.
connect.title: Connect
connect.lede: Connect your AI. Hoody works best from the AI you already use. Connect it once and it gets real computers, terminals, displays, browsers and files.
skills.title: Skills
skills.lede: A skill is a file that teaches a coding agent how Hoody's HTTP API works: which calls exist and how to make them. It gives no access by itself; a key or a sign-in does that.
skills.installBody: Run one of these in the folder where you use your agent. The tool asks which of your agents to add the skill to.
skills.cap.repo: The same skill with every docs page on disk
skills.cap.global: For every project on this device
skills.node: npx comes with Node.js. The skills tool needs Node.js 22.20 or newer.
skills.review: A skill runs with your agent's full permissions. Read what you install; the Hoody skill is plain text.
skills.agentsMore: The tool knows other agents too. Each installs the same way, with its name after -a.
skills.builtIn: The Hoody agent on your computers ships with the Hoody skills.
skills.checkBody: List the skills the tool installed, then ask your agent something the skill answers.
skills.prompt: Using the Hoody skill, list my Hoody computers and their status.
skills.updateBody: The tool tracks an install from HoodyNetwork/hoody-sdk: check for a new version and update it with the first two lines. It does not track an install from the skill address; run that add command again for the latest.
skills.signInBody: Make a key on the Keys page and give it to the agent as HOODY_TOKEN in the shell it runs in. With the SDK, pass it as token. The hoody CLI reads HOODY_TOKEN too. Or sign the CLI in with your account with the sign-in line of the CLI door under Connect; if you signed in to another platform before, sign in again. Add --base-url only when you use another platform.
build.title: Build your own
build.lede: The Hub has no private powers. Every page here calls Hoody's public HTTP API. Your own page, script or agent can make the same calls, within what its key or sign-in may do, so you can build the interface you want, or run your account from your own agents.
build.step1: Open your browser's developer tools: F12, or Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows and Linux, or Cmd+Option+I on macOS. Chrome and Firefox both have them.
build.step2: Open the Network tab and pick the Fetch/XHR filter (XHR in Firefox).
build.step3: Use the Hub as usual. Each new row is one call. Click it to see its method, address and headers, and the JSON it answered under Response.
build.token: The Authorization header carries your session token. Anyone who has it can act as you until it expires: never paste it into a chat, an issue or a screenshot.
build.find: To find the call behind something the Hub shows, do it in the Hub with the Network tab open, then give your agent the method and address.
build.sameBody: These all list your computers. Use a key from the Keys page, never the session token.
build.cap.agent: An agent with the Hoody skill
build.dashboard: Build a dashboard with your agent
build.d1: Install the Hoody skill in your coding agent.
build.d2: Make a key on the Keys page and set it in the shell the agent runs in:
build.d2.label: Set your key
build.d3: Open the agent in an empty folder and say what you want, for example:
build.d3.label: Example prompt
build.prompt: Using the Hoody skill, build a dashboard for my Hoody account that runs on this machine. A small local server reads HOODY_TOKEN from the environment and calls the Hoody API. The page lists my computers with their status and links, and never receives the token.
build.d4: Run it on your own machine. A computer's URLs open for anyone who has them until you set permissions, so move a dashboard that holds your key to a computer only after you protect it.
build.d5: Keep asking in plain words: add your Bots, your files or your logs. Each one is more HTTP calls, to the account API or to the programs on your computer.

door.ai.note: Paste this into an AI that can open links. It can guide you through connecting Hoody.
door.coding.note: The skill teaches your AI how Hoody works. A key gives it access.
door.sdk.note: Keep your account key out of browser code and source files.
door.http.note: Account API calls use your key. Computer links follow their link permissions.
door.mcp.note: Your Bot provides the MCP endpoint.
door.models.note: OpenAI-compatible apps use the base with /v1. Anthropic-compatible apps use the base without it.
door.chat.note: In the Agent app, select your Bot and open Connect, then Chat apps.
door.chat.path: Bots → Connect → Chat apps → Add chat app
door.ssh.note: Opens the Hoody CLI and Agent without a local installation.
links.title: Every link
links.lede: Every program of the picked computer has its own address. Anyone with an address can reach that program, so share them only with people you have given access to.
bots.title: Bots
bots.lede: Talk to a Bot from a chat app, an AI app or its own link. It runs agent sessions and reports back.
tools.title: Tools
tool.agent: Your AI next to your files. Watch it, steer it.
tool.terminal: A full shell in a tab, shared with your agent.
tool.screen: The computer's desktop, live, on any device.
tool.files: Browse, edit and download what is on disk.
tool.browser: A real browser your agent can drive.
tool.board: Your own grid of tools, side by side.
tool.board.name: Board
tool.bots: Give your agent a link, a QR and keys.
tool.moreBody: Code, SQLite, Pipe, Exec, Cron and others. Open any of them from Programs.

try.title: Try this
recipe.1: Watch your agent drive a browser
recipe.1.body: Ask it to test your site, then watch it work in the Browser.
recipe.1.board: Ask it to test your site, then put Agent and Browser side by side on a Board.
recipe.2: Give a Bot to your team with a QR
recipe.2.body: New Bot, then scan the code with a phone. Each person gets a named key.
recipe.3: Keep each client in its own realm
recipe.3.body: Name a realm, then pick it from the realm menu at the top (on a phone, tap the realm square). Everything here follows it.
recipe.4: Jump to any computer or program
recipe.4.body: Press Ctrl K and type part of its name.
recipe.5: Use a Bot from the OpenAI SDK
recipe.5.body: Copy its /v1 base and a key. Any OpenAI app can call it.
recipe.6.body: Home shows the computer picked in the top bar and each program on it.
realms.title: Realms
realms.lede: One realm per client, project or experiment. Pick a realm from the realm menu at the top (on a phone, tap the realm square) and every list and new thing follows it. Keys can be limited to one realm, so an agent you connect for a client sees only that client.
topics.title: Topics
topics.lede: Short explanations from the pages of the Hub.
keys.title: Keyboard
look.title: Look
look.body: Light or dark is in the account menu, under Appearance. It is saved in this browser only.
state.unknown: Some facts could not be read, so some lines show as not filled in. Nothing was changed.
state.noComputer: No computer is picked, so lines that need one are not filled in.
state.noRealmComputers: This realm has no computers yet.
demo.topic.what.title: What a script is
demo.topic.what.body: A script is a small program on your computer. It answers a web address, or runs on its own on a schedule.
demo.topic.key.title: Callers need a key
demo.topic.key.body: New scripts need a key. Apps send it with each call, so only they can run the script.
demo.topic.snap.title: Notes and snapshots
demo.topic.snap.body: A computer's snapshots include its notes once they have reached the computer.
